text: Sentinel ships a gallery of pre-built workbook templates, under Threat Management, Workbooks, Templates. These aren't generic security dashboards -- each one is built for a specific data source and only becomes useful once the matching data connector, from Chapter 1, is actually ingesting that data into the Log Analytics workspace behind it.

The Azure AD Sign-in Logs workbook visualizes authentication activity -- successful and failed sign-ins over time, sign-ins by location, risky sign-in trends -- but it has nothing to show until the Microsoft Entra ID connector is enabled and sign-in data is flowing in. The Office 365 template follows the same pattern, surfacing mailbox access, file activity, and Teams usage only once that connector is sending telemetry.

Using a built-in workbook is close to a one-click action: find the template matching a connector you already have enabled, click Save, and it's added to your Workbooks list, already wired to the right tables and columns. For a standard question like sign-in trends, activating the template is almost always the right first move -- Microsoft has already solved it, so there's no reason to write the same KQL from scratch.

A built-in workbook stops being enough the moment a question is specific to your organization. A SOC lead wanting failed-login trends cross-referenced against this company's own VIP account list -- executives, domain admins -- won't find that in any Microsoft template, because Microsoft has no way to know that list. That gap is exactly what a custom workbook is for.

A custom workbook can start from a completely blank canvas, or from cloning and editing a built-in template, which Sentinel allows and which is often faster than starting from nothing. Either way, the result is a workbook built around the specific KQL query steps, parameters, and layout a built-in template was never going to anticipate. Next up, Lesson 15 looks at how the query results inside either kind of workbook actually turn into a chart in the first place.
